sections.sectionText: Meets with CW 202-D. In Storymaking, we’ll explore the rich range of craft across the spectrum of contemporary narrative arts: fiction, film, video games, graphic novels, television, picture books, theater—all art forms centered around story. Working from a creator’s point of view, we’ll deconstruct the storytelling tools, techniques, and processes used in these varied narrative fields, while also emphasizing foundational concepts of storymaking across form and genre. We will read and watch and listen and play. We will break down film scenes, close-read short fiction, explore ludonarrative game arcs, and contemplate many other form-specific aspects of storycraft. We’ll examine multi-form adaptations such as The Last of Us, Jaws, and The Talented Mr. Ripley. We’ll have guests visiting class from time to time, working practitioners in their narrative fields. Although not a workshop, Storymaking culminates in a final project in a narrative form chosen by the student and instructor, to be shared with the class.

One Little Spark: Disney Storytelling, Culture, and Fandom: From theme parks to video games, hand-drawn animation to mascot characters, the Walt Disney Company was formed through a “journey into imagination” by pioneering and experimenting with storytelling in various forms, cultivating devoted fans and creating a media empire. In 2024, the Walt Disney Company brought in $91 billion through these entertainment ventures. How did the Disney brand use storytelling to establish such prominent cultural dominance? This course will critically explore Disney’s socio-economic and cultural impacts through analysis of its theme parks, theatrical offerings/licensing, and fan behavior.

sections.sectionText: Clowning the Classics—Adapting The Suppliants: This course begins with an introduction to clowning and devised theatre, using the fundamentals of clown and collaborative creation as tools for adaptation and performance. Students then apply these techniques to reimagine Aeschylus’ The Suppliants—a story of flight, trauma, and resilience that remains urgent and relevant today. In the second half of the semester, students collaborate with Paul O’Mahony (Out of Chaos Theatre, U.K.), Kim McKean (Theatre), and Angeliki Tzanetou (Classics) to write, rehearse, and perform their adaptation. This interdisciplinary collaboration culminates in a public presentation. Regular Meetings: (1/20/26-5/6/26) M,W; 3:00-4:20p Rehearsal Schedule: (4/6/26-4/15/26) M,T,W; 6:00-10:00p (4/10/26-4/17/26) F; 2:00-5:00p (4/18/26) Sat; 2:00-7:00p (4/20/26-4/25/26) M,T,W,R,F,Sat; 6:00-10:00p

sections.sectionText: The Themed Entertainment Scenic Design Lab is a collaborative, project-based course. Throughout the semester, students will explore the scenic design process specifically for environments found in themed entertainment. Hands-on individual and collaborative projects will allow participants to gain practical experience in developing and executing scenic concepts for theoretical attractions. The main project in this course will guide students through the phases of designing the environment for a major themed attraction—such as a dark ride— from Bluesky concept ideation to schematic design, with storytelling at the core of the process.
